KNOWLEDGE GRAPH FOR FL-101 — human-reviewed facts, each with its source.

FAULT: Underfill  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 11 and 12.1]
  early warning: If the checkweigher rejects more than 1 bottle in 100 over an hour, tell the shift lead. A rising reject count is often the first sign of worn seals.
  correct response: Press STOP (normal stop, not the emergency stop unless someone is in danger). Dripping valve: call the maintenance technician to replace the seal kit using WI-FL101-001. No dripping: lock out the machine and clean that valve's nozzle. Then check the product supply pressure.
  alarm message: Fill level low — bottles under target volume
  first check: Read the checkweigher report: it shows which valve numbers are underfilling. Look at those valves for dripping.
  causes in order: 1. Worn fill valve seal (the valve drips between fills). 2. Blocked fill nozzle (no dripping). 3. Low product supply pressure (see Product Supply Pressure Low).
  frequency: The most common alarm on FL-101
  alarm trigger: The alarm starts when the checkweigher rejects 3 underfilled bottles in a row
  wrong response: increase the fill time to make up for underfill. It hides worn seals and causes overflow and spillage (NCR-2026-012)
  systemic rule: Three or more underfill alarms in one shift means a systemic fault, usually several worn seals. Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor.
  definition: A bottle with less than 495 ml
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Volume Specification: allowed range: 495 to 505 ml — the checkweigher rejects anything outside this; hourly check: Every hour, take 5 bottles off the line and weigh them by hand; all must be in range; checkweigher test: Before starting, the 490 ml and 510 ml test bottles must be rejected and the 500 ml bottle must pass. If not, do not start: call the quality lead.; target: 500 ml  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.4, 10 and 11]
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Time Setting: rule: The fill time must NOT be changed by operators. Changing it needs written approval from engineering. A longer fill time does not fix underfill: it hides the real cause and makes bottles overflow.; setting: 3.2 seconds, factory set  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 10]
  Possible causes:
    - Worn Fill Valve Seal  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.1 and 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Sections 3 and 9, NCR-2026-012 Section 5]
        service interval: Every 3 months or 1,500 running hours, whichever comes first
        check: The checkweigher report shows which valves are underfilling. A valve that drips between fills has a worn seal.
        symptom: The valve drips between fills
        signs of wear: Flattened on one side, small cracks at the edge, hard instead of soft, a groove in the sealing face, discoloured or swollen
        ncr reference: NCR-2026-012: seals on valves 7, 12, 13 and 19 were 900 running hours past the 1,500-hour limit
        many worn: If more than 4 seals are badly worn at the same time, tell the maintenance supervisor: the replacement interval may be too long
        part: SEAL-FV-24
            minimum stock: 10 kits
            description: Fill valve seal kit: main seal and O-ring, one per valve
            location: Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2
        fix: Fill Valve Seal Replacement  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 2 to 8 and 11]
            lubricant rule: Only food-grade lubricant FGL-1. Any other lubricant contaminates the product.
            when to replace: A valve drips between fills; the checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again; three or more underfill alarms in one shift; or the seal has reached 3 months or 1,500 running hours
            before you start: Check the checkweigher report to see which valves are underfilling, mark them with a green tag, and tell the shift lead how long the line will be stopped
            signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check before normal production restarts. Record the date, valve numbers, seal kits used, condition of the old seals, first-bottle results and your name in the maintenance log.
            steps: 1. Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO). 2. Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level. 3. Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left). 4. Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick. 5. Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth and check it for scratches. 6. Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit with a thin layer of FGL-1 lubricant. 7. Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks). 8. Count the tools and parts on the tray, remove the lock and refill the bowl. 9. Sanitation rinse (mandatory). 10. First-bottle check (mandatory).
            reference: WI-FL101-001
            important note: For the first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change, bottles may be slightly overfilled (up to 510 ml) while the new seals settle. This is EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR — not a fault. Do not change any settings.
            scratched seat: A scratched valve seat must be reported to the maintenance supervisor: a new seal will not seal on a scratched seat
            time: One valve about 15 minutes; a typical job (1 to 4 valves) 30 to 45 minutes
            total downtime: about 1 hour including the rinse and the first-bottle check
            who: Trained maintenance technicians only
            then required: Sanitation Rinse  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 9, FL-101-SOP Sections 4, 9, 12.3 and 17]
                method: Rinse the bowl, valves and nozzles with clean water for 10 minutes. This removes lubricant and particles from the new seals.
                also required: At start-up if the machine has been stopped for more than 4 hours, after glass breakage, and at the end of every shift
                mandatory: true — never skip it after a seal change: the first bottles would carry lubricant into the product
            then required: First-Bottle Check  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 10 and Section 11]
                method: Run at normal speed and weigh the first 20 bottles. All 20 must be between 495 and 505 ml. If any bottle is outside this range, stop and check the valve again.
                signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check
                mandatory: true — normal production must not restart without it
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003)  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 6.2]
                lock rule: Only the person who fitted a lock may remove it
                required before: Any maintenance, clearing a jam, changing parts, or reaching into the machine
                steps: 1. Switch off power at the main isolator. 2. Lock the isolator with your personal padlock. 3. Tag it with your name and the date. 4. Try to start the machine to prove it cannot run.
        known pattern: Fill Time Trap  [source: NCR-2026-012 Sections 5 and 8]
            chain: Worn seals drip → underfill alarms → fill time raised 3.2 → 3.6 → 3.9 s → most valves overflow → spillage and wet labels → 1,200 bottles rejected, 2 hours 10 minutes downtime
            correct response: Underfill is a seal problem until proven otherwise: check for dripping valves first and replace worn seals (WI-FL101-001). Leave the fill time at the factory setting.
            wrong response: raise the fill time to fix underfill
            description: The operator raises the fill time to make up for underfill caused by worn seals, and most valves then overflow
            lesson from: NCR-2026-012, night shift of 16 January 2026
    - Blocked Fill Nozzle  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
        symptom: The valve underfills but does not drip: debris in the nozzle
        fix: Fill Nozzle Cleaning  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1 Step 4, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
            method: Lock out the machine and clean the nozzle of the underfilling valve
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)
  pattern: Fill Time Trap (details above)
  pattern: Systemic Underfill Indicator  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 12.1 and 13, NCR-2026-012 Section 8]
      correct response: Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor
      meaning: Several worn seals: a systemic fault, not bad luck
      trigger: 3 or more underfill alarms in one shift
      then required: Fill Valve Seal Replacement (details above)
      then required: Escalate to Maintenance Supervisor  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 13]
          electrical rule: Do not attempt electrical repairs. Always call maintenance.
          trigger 3: Any electrical fault code shows on the control panel
          trigger 4: A guide rail will not lock in position
          trigger 5: Any glass breakage (also call the quality lead)
          trigger 1: The same alarm happens 3 or more times in one shift
          trigger 2: Underfill continues after the seals have been replaced

FAULT: Overfill  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 8 and 10, FL-101-SOP Section 4, NCR-2026-012 Section 5]
  symptom: Bottles above 505 ml, overfilling or overflowing; the checkweigher rejects them
  definition: A bottle with more than 505 ml
  first check: Was a seal change done in the last few minutes? If the overfill stops within 2 to 3 minutes, it is normal settling: take no action and do not change any settings.
  causes in order: 1. New seals settling in the first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change (expected, not a fault). 2. Valve not fully clicked in (overfill still there after 5 minutes). 3. Fill time raised above the factory setting (NCR-2026-012).
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Volume Specification: allowed range: 495 to 505 ml — the checkweigher rejects anything outside this; hourly check: Every hour, take 5 bottles off the line and weigh them by hand; all must be in range; checkweigher test: Before starting, the 490 ml and 510 ml test bottles must be rejected and the 500 ml bottle must pass. If not, do not start: call the quality lead.; target: 500 ml  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.4, 10 and 11]
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Time Setting: rule: The fill time must NOT be changed by operators. Changing it needs written approval from engineering. A longer fill time does not fix underfill: it hides the real cause and makes bottles overflow.; setting: 3.2 seconds, factory set  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 10]
  Possible causes:
    - New Seals Settling  [source: WI-FL101-001 Section 8 (IMPORTANT note) and Section 10]
        when: The first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change
        expected behaviour: Bottles may be slightly overfilled (up to 510 ml) while the new seals settle. This is EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR — not a fault. Do not change any settings. The checkweigher rejects these bottles automatically.
        fix: First-Bottle Check (details above)
    - Valve Not Fully Clicked In  [source: WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
        symptom: Overfill still there after 5 minutes following a seal change
        fix: Refit the Fill Valve  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 7 and Section 10]
            method: Refit the valve: quarter turn to the right until it clicks
            when: Overfill is still there 5 minutes after a seal change
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)
    - Fill Time Raised Above Factory Setting  [source: NCR-2026-012 Sections 1 and 5]
        effect: Most valves overflow: water spills onto the bottles and conveyor, and labels get wet and peel
        ncr reference: NCR-2026-012: the fill time was raised from 3.2 to 3.6, then 3.9 seconds; 1,200 bottles were rejected
        fix: Restore Fill Time to Factory Setting  [source: NCR-2026-012 Section 7, FL-101-SOP Section 10]
            method: Maintenance restores the fill time to the factory setting
            rule: Operators must not change the fill time. Any change needs written approval from engineering.
        known pattern: Fill Time Trap (details above)

FAULT: Infeed Jam  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.2]
  safety rule: Never reach into the infeed or the star wheel while the machine is running. Stop the machine and lock it out before clearing any jam.
  alarm message: Infeed jam — bottles stopped at infeed
  if a bottle breaks: If a bottle breaks during a jam, stop and follow SOP Section 12.3.
  first check: If a changeover happened this shift, check the changeover record first.
  causes in order: 1. Guide rails not reset after a bottle size changeover. 2. Chipped or damaged bottles. 3. Bottle feed conveyor running too fast.
  SPECIFICATION — Guide Rail Setting: reference: Changeover sheet CS-FL101; bottle 500 ml: Rail position A; bottle 330 ml: Rail position B; also check: Rails locked and the matching star wheel fitted  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.2 and 14]
  SPECIFICATION — Line Speed: normal: 120 bottles per minute (maximum 130); start: Start at 60 bottles per minute, then raise to normal speed once the first bottles are in range  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 9 and 10]
  Possible causes:
    - Guide Rails Not Reset After Changeover  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.2, 12.2 and 14]
        note: Most infeed jams in the first hour after a changeover come from rails left in the wrong position
        check: Check the guide rail position matches the bottle size, and that the rails are locked
        fix: Bottle Size Changeover  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 14]
            steps: 1. Lock out the machine. 2. Move the guide rails to the position on changeover sheet CS-FL101 and lock them. 3. Fit the matching star wheel. 4. Remove the lock and run 20 bottles at 60 bottles per minute. 5. Check none jam and all fill correctly, then return to normal speed. 6. Record the changeover in the shift log; the shift lead signs the changeover record.
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)
    - Chipped or Damaged Bottles  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.2]
        fix: Remove any chipped or damaged bottles from the infeed, wearing cut-resistant gloves
        fix: Infeed Jam Clearing  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.2]
            steps: 1. Press STOP. 2. Lock out the machine. 3. Remove the jammed bottles wearing cut-resistant gloves. 4. Check the guide rail position matches the bottle size, and reset the rails if they are wrong. 5. Remove any chipped or damaged bottles from the infeed. 6. Remove the lock, restart at 60 bottles per minute for 2 minutes, then return to normal speed.
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)
    - Bottle Feed Conveyor Running Too Fast  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.2]
        note: Third most common cause of infeed jams. The SOP gives no specific fix for it.
  procedure: Infeed Jam Clearing (details above)
  procedure: Escalate to Maintenance Supervisor (details above)

FAULT: Glass Breakage  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 12.3 and 13]
  quality impact: Every bottle filled in the last 30 minutes goes on QA HOLD, and open bottles within 2 metres of the break are thrown away
  symptom: Broken glass on the star wheel, inside the filler or near the line
  who to call: The quality lead and the maintenance supervisor, for any glass breakage
  alarm message: Glass breakage detected in filler
  criticality: CRITICAL — broken glass can end up inside filled bottles. This is a product safety event. Follow GBP-001 (Glass and Brittle Plastics Policy).
  Possible causes:
    - Bottle Broken During a Jam  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 12.2 and 12.3]
        note: If a bottle breaks during a jam, stop and follow the glass breakage steps
        fix: Glass Breakage Response  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.3]
            reference: GBP-001 Glass and Brittle Plastics Policy
            cleanup rule: Never use compressed air: air spreads glass
            steps: 1. Stop the line at once with the emergency stop. 2. Do not open any guard until the machine has stopped and is locked out. 3. Put every bottle filled in the last 30 minutes on QA HOLD; throw away open bottles within 2 metres of the break. 4. Clean up with the red glass kit only, using a vacuum. 5. Run the sanitation rinse (10 minutes). 6. The quality lead signs off before the line restarts. 7. Record the event in the glass breakage log.
            then required: Sanitation Rinse (details above)
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)
  procedure: Glass Breakage Response (details above)
  procedure: Escalate to Maintenance Supervisor (details above)
  safety: QA HOLD  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 4 and 12.3]
      release: Bottles on QA HOLD may only be released after the quality lead has inspected them
      action: Label the held bottles QA HOLD: do not ship until the quality lead has checked them

FAULT: Product Supply Pressure Low  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.4]
  effect: Low supply pressure makes bottles underfill
  alarm message: Product supply pressure low — below 1.3 bar
  causes in order: 1. Supply filter blocked. 2. Air in the supply line. 3. Supply tank running low.
  SPECIFICATION — Product Supply Pressure Specification: alarm: Below 1.3 bar; normal range: 1.5 to 2.0 bar  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.3 and 10]
  Possible causes:
    - Supply Filter Blocked  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.3 and 12.4]
        service interval: Cleaned once a week. Check the date on the filter tag.
        fix: Clean or replace the supply filter (FLT-PS-10)
        part: FLT-PS-10
            description: Product supply filter
        fix: Supply Pressure Restore  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.4]
            steps: 1. Press STOP. 2. Clean the supply filter. 3. Bleed air from the supply line. 4. Confirm the pressure is back in range. 5. Restart, then weigh the first 20 bottles: all must be within the allowed fill range.
    - Air in the Supply Line  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.4]
        fix: Bleed the air using the bleed valve on the bowl
        fix: Supply Pressure Restore (details above)
    - Supply Tank Running Low  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.4]
        fix: Check the tank level with the water treatment room
        fix: Supply Pressure Restore (details above)
  procedure: Supply Pressure Restore (details above)

Machine-wide safety (applies to any work on this machine):
  LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)
  PPE Required on Filling Line 1  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 6.1]
      feet: Safety shoes
      hands: Cut-resistant gloves when handling glass or change parts

   - The documented specification is the one to follow. Use ONLY its value in the steps.
   - Never write an instruction that sets, resets or targets the operator's value. It may be mentioned in the findings as a contradiction to review - never in HOW TO ADDRESS IT.

KNOWLEDGE GRAPH FOR FL-101 — human-reviewed facts, each with its source.

FAULT: Underfill  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 11 and 12.1]
  early warning: If the checkweigher rejects more than 1 bottle in 100 over an hour, tell the shift lead. A rising reject count is often the first sign of worn seals.
  correct response: Press STOP (normal stop, not the emergency stop unless someone is in danger). Dripping valve: call the maintenance technician to replace the seal kit using WI-FL101-001. No dripping: lock out the machine and clean that valve's nozzle. Then check the product supply pressure.
  alarm message: Fill level low — bottles under target volume
  first check: Read the checkweigher report: it shows which valve numbers are underfilling. Look at those valves for dripping.
  causes in order: 1. Worn fill valve seal (the valve drips between fills). 2. Blocked fill nozzle (no dripping). 3. Low product supply pressure (see Product Supply Pressure Low).

FAULT: Overfill  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 8 and 10, FL-101-SOP Section 4, NCR-2026-012 Section 5]
  symptom: Bottles above 505 ml, overfilling or overflowing; the checkweigher rejects them
  definition: A bottle with more than 505 ml
  first check: Was a seal change done in the last few minutes? If the overfill stops within 2 to 3 minutes, it is normal settling: take no action and do not change any settings.
  causes in order: 1. New seals settling in the first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change (expected, not a fault). 2. Valve not fully clicked in (overfill still there after 5 minutes). 3. Fill time raised above the factory setting (NCR-2026-012).
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Volume Specification: allowed range: 495 to 505 ml — the checkweigher rejects anything outside this; hourly check: Every hour, take 5 bottles off the line and weigh them by hand; all must be in range; checkweigher test: Before starting, the 490 ml and 510 ml test bottles must be rejected and the 500 ml bottle must pass. If not, do not start: call the quality lead.; target: 500 ml  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.4, 10 and 11]
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Time Setting: rule: The fill time must NOT be changed by operators. Changing it needs written approval from engineering. A longer fill time does not fix underfill: it hides the real cause and makes bottles overflow.; setting: 3.2 seconds, factory set  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 10]
  Possible causes:
    - New Seals Settling  [source: WI-FL101-001 Section 8 (IMPORTANT note) and Section 10]
        when: The first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change
        expected behaviour: Bottles may be slightly overfilled (up to 510 ml) while the new seals settle. This is EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR — not a fault. Do not change any settings. The checkweigher rejects these bottles automatically.
        fix: First-Bottle Check (details above)
    - Valve Not Fully Clicked In  [source: WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
        symptom: Overfill still there after 5 minutes following a seal change
        fix: Refit the Fill Valve  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 7 and Section 10]
            method: Refit the valve: quarter turn to the right until it clicks
            when: Overfill is still there 5 minutes after a seal change
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)
    - Fill Time Raised Above Factory Setting  [source: NCR-2026-012 Sections 1 and 5]
        effect: Most valves overflow: water spills onto the bottles and conveyor, and labels get wet and peel
        ncr reference: NCR-2026-012: the fill time was raised from 3.2 to 3.6, then 3.9 seconds; 1,200 bottles were rejected
        fix: Restore Fill Time to Factory Setting  [source: NCR-2026-012 Section 7, FL-101-SOP Section 10]
            method: Maintenance restores the fill time to the factory setting
            rule: Operators must not change the fill time. Any change needs written approval from engineering.
        known pattern: Fill Time Trap (details above)

FAULT: Infeed Jam  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.2]
  safety rule: Never reach into the infeed or the star wheel while the machine is running. Stop the machine and lock it out before clearing any jam.
  alarm message: Infeed jam — bottles stopped at infeed
  if a bottle breaks: If a bottle breaks during a jam, stop and follow SOP Section 12.3.
  first check: If a changeover happened this shift, check the changeover record first.
  causes in order: 1. Guide rails not reset after a bottle size changeover. 2. Chipped or damaged bottles. 3. Bottle feed conveyor running too fast.
  SPECIFICATION — Guide Rail Setting: reference: Changeover sheet CS-FL101; bottle 500 ml: Rail position A; bottle 330 ml: Rail position B; also check: Rails locked and the matching star wheel fitted  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.2 and 14]
  SPECIFICATION — Line Speed: normal: 120 bottles per minute (maximum 130); start: Start at 60 bottles per minute, then raise to normal speed once the first bottles are in range  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 9 and 10]
  Possible causes:
    - Guide Rails Not Reset After Changeover  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.2, 12.2 and 14]
        note: Most infeed jams in the first hour after a changeover come from rails left in the wrong position
        check: Check the guide rail position matches the bottle size, and that the rails are locked
        fix: Bottle Size Changeover  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 14]
            steps: 1. Lock out the machine. 2. Move the guide rails to the position on changeover sheet CS-FL101 and lock them. 3. Fit the matching star wheel. 4. Remove the lock and run 20 bottles at 60 bottles per minute. 5. Check none jam and all fill correctly, then return to normal speed. 6. Record the changeover in the shift log; the shift lead signs the changeover record.
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)
    - Chipped or Damaged Bottles  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.2]
        fix: Remove any chipped or damaged bottles from the infeed, wearing cut-resistant gloves
        fix: Infeed Jam Clearing  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.2]
            steps: 1. Press STOP. 2. Lock out the machine. 3. Remove the jammed bottles wearing cut-resistant gloves. 4. Check the guide rail position matches the bottle size, and reset the rails if they are wrong. 5. Remove any chipped or damaged bottles from the infeed. 6. Remove the lock, restart at 60 bottles per minute for 2 minutes, then return to normal speed.
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)
    - Bottle Feed Conveyor Running Too Fast  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.2]
        note: Third most common cause of infeed jams. The SOP gives no specific fix for it.
  procedure: Infeed Jam Clearing (details above)
  procedure: Escalate to Maintenance Supervisor (details above)

  quality impact: Every bottle filled in the last 30 minutes goes on QA HOLD, and open bottles within 2 metres of the break are thrown away
  symptom: Broken glass on the star wheel, inside the filler or near the line
  who to call: The quality lead and the maintenance supervisor, for any glass breakage
  alarm message: Glass breakage detected in filler
  criticality: CRITICAL — broken glass can end up inside filled bottles. This is a product safety event. Follow GBP-001 (Glass and Brittle Plastics Policy).
  Possible causes:
    - Bottle Broken During a Jam  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 12.2 and 12.3]

            reference: GBP-001 Glass and Brittle Plastics Policy

            steps: 1. Stop the line at once with the emergency stop. 2. Do not open any guard until the machine has stopped and is locked out. 3. Put every bottle filled in the last 30 minutes on QA HOLD; throw away open bottles within 2 metres of the break. 4. Clean up with the red glass kit only, using a vacuum. 5. Run the sanitation rinse (10 minutes). 6. The quality lead signs off before the line restarts. 7. Record the event in the glass breakage log.
            then required: Sanitation Rinse (details above)
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)
  procedure: Glass Breakage Response (details above)
  procedure: Escalate to Maintenance Supervisor (details above)
  safety: QA HOLD  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 4 and 12.3]
      release: Bottles on QA HOLD may only be released after the quality lead has inspected them
      action: Label the held bottles QA HOLD: do not ship until the quality lead has checked them

FAULT: Product Supply Pressure Low  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.4]
  effect: Low supply pressure makes bottles underfill
  alarm message: Product supply pressure low — below 1.3 bar
  causes in order: 1. Supply filter blocked. 2. Air in the supply line. 3. Supply tank running low.
  SPECIFICATION — Product Supply Pressure Specification: alarm: Below 1.3 bar; normal range: 1.5 to 2.0 bar  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.3 and 10]
  Possible causes:
    - Supply Filter Blocked  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.3 and 12.4]
        service interval: Cleaned once a week. Check the date on the filter tag.
        fix: Clean or replace the supply filter (FLT-PS-10)
        part: FLT-PS-10
            description: Product supply filter
        fix: Supply Pressure Restore  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.4]
            steps: 1. Press STOP. 2. Clean the supply filter. 3. Bleed air from the supply line. 4. Confirm the pressure is back in range. 5. Restart, then weigh the first 20 bottles: all must be within the allowed fill range.

    - Supply Tank Running Low  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.4]
        fix: Check the tank level with the water treatment room
        fix: Supply Pressure Restore (details above)

KNOWLEDGE GRAPH FOR FL-101 — human-reviewed facts, each with its source.

FAULT: Underfill  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 11 and 12.1]
  early warning: If the checkweigher rejects more than 1 bottle in 100 over an hour, tell the shift lead. A rising reject count is often the first sign of worn seals.
  correct response: Press STOP (normal stop, not the emergency stop unless someone is in danger). Dripping valve: call the maintenance technician to replace the seal kit using WI-FL101-001. No dripping: lock out the machine and clean that valve's nozzle. Then check the product supply pressure.
  alarm message: Fill level low — bottles under target volume
  first check: Read the checkweigher report: it shows which valve numbers are underfilling. Look at those valves for dripping.
  causes in order: 1. Worn fill valve seal (the valve drips between fills). 2. Blocked fill nozzle (no dripping). 3. Low product supply pressure (see Product Supply Pressure Low).
  frequency: The most common alarm on FL-101
  alarm trigger: The alarm starts when the checkweigher rejects 3 underfilled bottles in a row
  wrong response: increase the fill time to make up for underfill. It hides worn seals and causes overflow and spillage (NCR-2026-012)
  systemic rule: Three or more underfill alarms in one shift means a systemic fault, usually several worn seals. Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor.
  definition: A bottle with less than 495 ml
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Volume Specification: allowed range: 495 to 505 ml — the checkweigher rejects anything outside this; hourly check: Every hour, take 5 bottles off the line and weigh them by hand; all must be in range; checkweigher test: Before starting, the 490 ml and 510 ml test bottles must be rejected and the 500 ml bottle must pass. If not, do not start: call the quality lead.; target: 500 ml  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.4, 10 and 11]
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Time Setting: rule: The fill time must NOT be changed by operators. Changing it needs written approval from engineering. A longer fill time does not fix underfill: it hides the real cause and makes bottles overflow.; setting: 3.2 seconds, factory set  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 10]
  Possible causes:
    - Worn Fill Valve Seal  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.1 and 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Sections 3 and 9, NCR-2026-012 Section 5]
        service interval: Every 3 months or 1,500 running hours, whichever comes first
        check: The checkweigher report shows which valves are underfilling. A valve that drips between fills has a worn seal.
        symptom: The valve drips between fills
        signs of wear: Flattened on one side, small cracks at the edge, hard instead of soft, a groove in the sealing face, discoloured or swollen
        ncr reference: NCR-2026-012: seals on valves 7, 12, 13 and 19 were 900 running hours past the 1,500-hour limit
        many worn: If more than 4 seals are badly worn at the same time, tell the maintenance supervisor: the replacement interval may be too long
        part: SEAL-FV-24
            minimum stock: 10 kits
            description: Fill valve seal kit: main seal and O-ring, one per valve
            location: Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2
        fix: Fill Valve Seal Replacement  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 2 to 8 and 11]
            lubricant rule: Only food-grade lubricant FGL-1. Any other lubricant contaminates the product.
            when to replace: A valve drips between fills; the checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again; three or more underfill alarms in one shift; or the seal has reached 3 months or 1,500 running hours
            before you start: Check the checkweigher report to see which valves are underfilling, mark them with a green tag, and tell the shift lead how long the line will be stopped
            signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check before normal production restarts. Record the date, valve numbers, seal kits used, condition of the old seals, first-bottle results and your name in the maintenance log.
            steps: 1. Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO). 2. Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level. 3. Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left). 4. Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick. 5. Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth and check it for scratches. 6. Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit with a thin layer of FGL-1 lubricant. 7. Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks). 8. Count the tools and parts on the tray, remove the lock and refill the bowl. 9. Sanitation rinse (mandatory). 10. First-bottle check (mandatory).
            reference: WI-FL101-001
            important note: For the first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change, bottles may be slightly overfilled (up to 510 ml) while the new seals settle. This is EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR — not a fault. Do not change any settings.
            scratched seat: A scratched valve seat must be reported to the maintenance supervisor: a new seal will not seal on a scratched seat
            time: One valve about 15 minutes; a typical job (1 to 4 valves) 30 to 45 minutes
            total downtime: about 1 hour including the rinse and the first-bottle check
            who: Trained maintenance technicians only
            then required: Sanitation Rinse  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 9, FL-101-SOP Sections 4, 9, 12.3 and 17]
                method: Rinse the bowl, valves and nozzles with clean water for 10 minutes. This removes lubricant and particles from the new seals.
                also required: At start-up if the machine has been stopped for more than 4 hours, after glass breakage, and at the end of every shift
                mandatory: true — never skip it after a seal change: the first bottles would carry lubricant into the product
            then required: First-Bottle Check  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 10 and Section 11]
                method: Run at normal speed and weigh the first 20 bottles. All 20 must be between 495 and 505 ml. If any bottle is outside this range, stop and check the valve again.
                signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check
                mandatory: true — normal production must not restart without it
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003)  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 6.2]
                lock rule: Only the person who fitted a lock may remove it
                required before: Any maintenance, clearing a jam, changing parts, or reaching into the machine
                steps: 1. Switch off power at the main isolator. 2. Lock the isolator with your personal padlock. 3. Tag it with your name and the date. 4. Try to start the machine to prove it cannot run.
        known pattern: Fill Time Trap  [source: NCR-2026-012 Sections 5 and 8]
            chain: Worn seals drip → underfill alarms → fill time raised 3.2 → 3.6 → 3.9 s → most valves overflow → spillage and wet labels → 1,200 bottles rejected, 2 hours 10 minutes downtime
            correct response: Underfill is a seal problem until proven otherwise: check for dripping valves first and replace worn seals (WI-FL101-001). Leave the fill time at the factory setting.
            wrong response: raise the fill time to fix underfill
            description: The operator raises the fill time to make up for underfill caused by worn seals, and most valves then overflow
            lesson from: NCR-2026-012, night shift of 16 January 2026
    - Blocked Fill Nozzle  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
        symptom: The valve underfills but does not drip: debris in the nozzle
        fix: Fill Nozzle Cleaning  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1 Step 4, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
            method: Lock out the machine and clean the nozzle of the underfilling valve
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)
  pattern: Fill Time Trap (details above)
  pattern: Systemic Underfill Indicator  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 12.1 and 13, NCR-2026-012 Section 8]
      correct response: Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor
      meaning: Several worn seals: a systemic fault, not bad luck
      trigger: 3 or more underfill alarms in one shift
      then required: Fill Valve Seal Replacement (details above)
      then required: Escalate to Maintenance Supervisor  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 13]
          electrical rule: Do not attempt electrical repairs. Always call maintenance.
          trigger 3: Any electrical fault code shows on the control panel
          trigger 4: A guide rail will not lock in position
          trigger 5: Any glass breakage (also call the quality lead)
          trigger 1: The same alarm happens 3 or more times in one shift
          trigger 2: Underfill continues after the seals have been replaced

  definition: A bottle with more than 505 ml

If not, do not start: call the quality lead.; target: 500 ml  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.4, 10 and 11]
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Time Setting: rule: The fill time must NOT be changed by operators. Changing it needs written approval from engineering. A longer fill time does not fix underfill: it hides the real cause and makes bottles overflow.; setting: 3.2 seconds, factory set  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 10]
  Possible causes:
    - New Seals Settling  [source: WI-FL101-001 Section 8 (IMPORTANT note) and Section 10]
        when: The first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change
        expected behaviour: Bottles may be slightly overfilled (up to 510 ml) while the new seals settle. This is EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR — not a fault. Do not change any settings. The checkweigher rejects these bottles automatically.
        fix: First-Bottle Check (details above)
    - Valve Not Fully Clicked In  [source: WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
        symptom: Overfill still there after 5 minutes following a seal change
        fix: Refit the Fill Valve  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 7 and Section 10]

            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)

KNOWLEDGE GRAPH FOR FL-101 — human-reviewed facts, each with its source.

FAULT: Underfill  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 11 and 12.1]
  early warning: If the checkweigher rejects more than 1 bottle in 100 over an hour, tell the shift lead. A rising reject count is often the first sign of worn seals.
  correct response: Press STOP (normal stop, not the emergency stop unless someone is in danger). Dripping valve: call the maintenance technician to replace the seal kit using WI-FL101-001. No dripping: lock out the machine and clean that valve's nozzle. Then check the product supply pressure.
  alarm message: Fill level low — bottles under target volume
  first check: Read the checkweigher report: it shows which valve numbers are underfilling. Look at those valves for dripping.
  causes in order: 1. Worn fill valve seal (the valve drips between fills). 2. Blocked fill nozzle (no dripping). 3. Low product supply pressure (see Product Supply Pressure Low).
  frequency: The most common alarm on FL-101
  alarm trigger: The alarm starts when the checkweigher rejects 3 underfilled bottles in a row
  wrong response: increase the fill time to make up for underfill. It hides worn seals and causes overflow and spillage (NCR-2026-012)
  systemic rule: Three or more underfill alarms in one shift means a systemic fault, usually several worn seals. Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor.
  definition: A bottle with less than 495 ml
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Volume Specification: allowed range: 495 to 505 ml — the checkweigher rejects anything outside this; hourly check: Every hour, take 5 bottles off the line and weigh them by hand; all must be in range; checkweigher test: Before starting, the 490 ml and 510 ml test bottles must be rejected and the 500 ml bottle must pass. If not, do not start: call the quality lead.; target: 500 ml  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.4, 10 and 11]
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Time Setting: rule: The fill time must NOT be changed by operators. Changing it needs written approval from engineering. A longer fill time does not fix underfill: it hides the real cause and makes bottles overflow.; setting: 3.2 seconds, factory set  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 10]
  Possible causes:
    - Worn Fill Valve Seal  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.1 and 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Sections 3 and 9, NCR-2026-012 Section 5]
        service interval: Every 3 months or 1,500 running hours, whichever comes first
        check: The checkweigher report shows which valves are underfilling. A valve that drips between fills has a worn seal.
        symptom: The valve drips between fills
        signs of wear: Flattened on one side, small cracks at the edge, hard instead of soft, a groove in the sealing face, discoloured or swollen
        ncr reference: NCR-2026-012: seals on valves 7, 12, 13 and 19 were 900 running hours past the 1,500-hour limit
        many worn: If more than 4 seals are badly worn at the same time, tell the maintenance supervisor: the replacement interval may be too long
        part: SEAL-FV-24
            minimum stock: 10 kits
            description: Fill valve seal kit: main seal and O-ring, one per valve
            location: Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2
        fix: Fill Valve Seal Replacement  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 2 to 8 and 11]
            lubricant rule: Only food-grade lubricant FGL-1. Any other lubricant contaminates the product.
            when to replace: A valve drips between fills; the checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again; three or more underfill alarms in one shift; or the seal has reached 3 months or 1,500 running hours
            before you start: Check the checkweigher report to see which valves are underfilling, mark them with a green tag, and tell the shift lead how long the line will be stopped
            signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check before normal production restarts. Record the date, valve numbers, seal kits used, condition of the old seals, first-bottle results and your name in the maintenance log.
            steps: 1. Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO). 2. Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level. 3. Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left). 4. Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick. 5. Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth and check it for scratches. 6. Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit with a thin layer of FGL-1 lubricant. 7. Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks). 8. Count the tools and parts on the tray, remove the lock and refill the bowl. 9. Sanitation rinse (mandatory). 10. First-bottle check (mandatory).
            reference: WI-FL101-001
            important note: For the first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change, bottles may be slightly overfilled (up to 510 ml) while the new seals settle. This is EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR — not a fault. Do not change any settings.
            scratched seat: A scratched valve seat must be reported to the maintenance supervisor: a new seal will not seal on a scratched seat
            time: One valve about 15 minutes; a typical job (1 to 4 valves) 30 to 45 minutes
            total downtime: about 1 hour including the rinse and the first-bottle check
            who: Trained maintenance technicians only
            then required: Sanitation Rinse  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 9, FL-101-SOP Sections 4, 9, 12.3 and 17]
                method: Rinse the bowl, valves and nozzles with clean water for 10 minutes. This removes lubricant and particles from the new seals.
                also required: At start-up if the machine has been stopped for more than 4 hours, after glass breakage, and at the end of every shift
                mandatory: true — never skip it after a seal change: the first bottles would carry lubricant into the product
            then required: First-Bottle Check  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 10 and Section 11]
                method: Run at normal speed and weigh the first 20 bottles. All 20 must be between 495 and 505 ml. If any bottle is outside this range, stop and check the valve again.
                signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check
                mandatory: true — normal production must not restart without it
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003)  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 6.2]
                lock rule: Only the person who fitted a lock may remove it
                required before: Any maintenance, clearing a jam, changing parts, or reaching into the machine
                steps: 1. Switch off power at the main isolator. 2. Lock the isolator with your personal padlock. 3. Tag it with your name and the date. 4. Try to start the machine to prove it cannot run.
        known pattern: Fill Time Trap  [source: NCR-2026-012 Sections 5 and 8]
            chain: Worn seals drip → underfill alarms → fill time raised 3.2 → 3.6 → 3.9 s → most valves overflow → spillage and wet labels → 1,200 bottles rejected, 2 hours 10 minutes downtime
            correct response: Underfill is a seal problem until proven otherwise: check for dripping valves first and replace worn seals (WI-FL101-001). Leave the fill time at the factory setting.
            wrong response: raise the fill time to fix underfill
            description: The operator raises the fill time to make up for underfill caused by worn seals, and most valves then overflow
            lesson from: NCR-2026-012, night shift of 16 January 2026

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: Blocked fill nozzle on valve 12 causing underfill without dripping (SOP lists blocked nozzle as cause when no drip is observed) 
- Difference from history: First recorded alarm for valve 12; prior alarms involved dripping valves and underfill; no prior “no‑drip” symptom for this valve.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: Line must be stopped for normal stop, lock‑out, nozzle cleaning and verification; estimated downtime ~1 hour including sanitation rinse and first‑bottle check (knowledge‑graph estimate)
- Safety risk: LOW (no immediate hazard, but LOTO and PPE required)
- Financial impact: Potential loss of product from rejected bottles during alarm plus ~1 hour downtime; exact cost not quantified in data.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- MEDIUM – single underfill alarm requiring line stop and corrective action; not a recurring fault nor a safety event, but impacts production and product quality.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action:
  Step 1: Safety – Press normal STOP, then perform LOTO per SAF‑003 (switch off main isolator, apply personal lock, tag with name/date, verify lockout).
  Step 2: Diagnosis – Read the checkweigher report to confirm valve 12 underfilling; visually inspect valve 12 for dripping (none observed).
  Step 3: Fix – Lock out the machine and clean the nozzle of valve 12 (SOP Section 12.1, WI‑FL101‑001). Then check product supply pressure (Section 12.4); if pressure is below 1.5 bar, follow low‑pressure procedure: clean supply filter, bleed air, restore pressure to 1.5–2.0 bar.
  Step 4: Verify – Restart machine, weigh first 20 bottles; all must be 495–505 ml. If any bottle is out of range, repeat nozzle cleaning or raise a maintenance work order.
  Step 5: Quality – Quarantine any bottles produced during the alarm; record results in the shift log and maintenance log; sign off first‑bottle check.
- Root cause fix (permanent solution): Implement a scheduled nozzle cleaning for valve 12 and verify nozzle integrity during routine maintenance; monitor for pressure deviations.
- Preventive action: Add valve 12 to the regular nozzle‑inspection checklist; train operators to clean nozzles when underfill occurs without drip; track pressure trends and set an alarm if pressure falls below 1.5 bar.
- Who to notify: Shift lead, Maintenance Supervisor, Quality Lead.

            lubricant rule: Only food-grade lubricant FGL-1. Any other lubricant contaminates the product.
            when to replace: A valve drips between fills; the checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again; three or more underfill alarms in one shift; or the seal has reached 3 months or 1,500 running hours

INVESTIGATION REPORT
══════════════════════════════════════════════════

INVESTIGATION REPORT — TECHNICAL
═══════════════════════════════════════

REPORT CONFIDENCE:
- Level: HIGH (worked out by code from the evidence, not by the AI)
- Why: fault identified (Underfill), knowledge graph available, evidence from Alarm, NCR, SOP
- Engineer review: not needed


SOURCE DATA:
- FL‑101‑SOP.txt (Revision 1.0) – procedure for underfill response, safety steps, specifications
- FL‑101‑Work‑Instruction.txt – notes on blocked nozzle and worn seal criteria
- FL‑101‑NCR.txt – NCR‑2026‑012 closed on 16 Jan 2026, seal replacement on valve 12
- DemoBottling‑Shift‑Log‑2026‑09‑10‑Night.csv – three underfill alarms on 10 Sep 2026 (01:30, 03:20, 04:45)
- Knowledge‑Graph entry for FL‑101 (verified) – causes, correct response, specifications
- Operator incident report (Tue 6 Oct 2026) – checkweigher rejecting bottles from valve 12, no drips observed

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: blocked fill nozzle on valve 12 (no dripping, underfill alarm) – supported by SOP “blocked fill nozzle (no dripping)” as second‑most likely cause and by work instruction stating blocked nozzle produces underfill without drips.
- Difference vs history: prior underfill alarms (Sep 2026) were associated with dripping valves and worn seals; this incident shows no drip and involves valve 12, which had its seal replaced in Jan 2026, indicating a different failure mode.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: line stopped for cleaning and verification; estimated downtime ≈ 1 hour (including sanitation rinse and first‑bottle check).
- Safety risk: LOW (no hazardous material release, LOTO required but no injury).
- Financial impact: loss of production for ~1 hour plus labor for maintenance; exact cost not quantified in source data.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH – LOTO is required before any maintenance (mandatory safety step) and underfill alarms trigger product‑quality loss; rule “any fault requiring LOTO or production stop = HIGH minimum”.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action:
  Step 1: Safety – Press STOP (normal stop), apply LOTO per SAF‑003 (lock out main isolator, tag with name/date, verify machine cannot start).
  Step 2: Diagnosis – Lock out, then clean the nozzle of valve 12 (SOP Section 12.1, work instruction “blocked nozzle”).
  Step 3: Fix – After cleaning, check product‑supply pressure (SOP Section 12.4). If pressure < 1.3 bar, follow low‑pressure procedure: clean supply filter, bleed air, confirm pressure 1.5‑2.0 bar, then restart.
  Step 4: Verify – Perform first‑bottle check: run first 20 bottles, all must weigh 495‑505 ml. If any out of range, repeat nozzle cleaning or raise maintenance work order.
  Step 5: Quality – Quarantine the first 20 bottles until verification is complete; record results in the maintenance log and sign‑off by shift supervisor.
- Root cause fix (permanent solution): implement a scheduled nozzle‑cleaning check for all fill valves every 3 months (or 1 500 hours) and add nozzle‑clog monitoring to the preventive‑maintenance schedule.
- Preventive action: add a daily visual inspection of valve nozzles for debris; update the shift checklist to include “nozzle visual check” before start‑up; train operators on recognizing blocked‑nozzle symptoms.
- Who to notify: Maintenance supervisor, Shift lead, Quality lead (for first‑bottle check sign‑off).

PLANT MANAGER SUMMARY
═══════════════════════════════════════

ROOT CAUSE: Blocked fill nozzle on valve 12 is preventing proper fill volume.

ACTION REQUIRED: Lock out the machine, clean valve 12’s nozzle, verify product‑supply pressure, and complete the mandatory first‑bottle check before restarting.  
RISK IF NOT ACTIONED: Continued underfill will produce out‑of‑spec product, leading to quality rejects, possible batch quarantine, and extended downtime.

12.1 Underfill
Alarm message: "Fill level low — bottles under target volume"
The alarm starts when the checkweigher rejects 3 underfilled bottles in a row.

This is the most common alarm on FL-101. Causes, most common first:
  1. Worn fill valve seal — the valve drips between fills
  2. Blocked fill nozzle — debris in the nozzle, no dripping
  3. Low product supply pressure — see Section 12.4

---

12.4 Product Supply Pressure Low
Alarm message: "Product supply pressure low — below 1.3 bar"

Low supply pressure makes bottles underfill.

Causes, most common first:
  1. Supply filter blocked — clean or replace the filter (FLT-PS-10)
  2. Air in the supply line — bleed the air using the bleed valve on the bowl
  3. Supply tank running low — check the tank level with the water
     treatment room

Immediate action:
  Step 1 — Press STOP.
  Step 2 — Clean the supply filter.
  Step 3 — Bleed air from the supply line.
  Step 4 — Confirm the pressure is back to 1.5 to 2.0 bar.
  Step 5 — Restart, then weigh the first 20 bottles. All must be 495 to 505 ml.

- DemoBottling‑Shift‑Log‑2026‑09‑10‑Night.csv – reject count 14 per 1 000 (1.4 %) with underfill alarms
- Operator incident message (2026‑10‑06) – “Reject count’s been creeping up all morning. No alarms yet.”

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: early stage wear of fill‑valve seals causing a gradual increase in under‑fill rejects, identified by the SOP as the first warning sign of worn seals. (Evidence: SOP “early warning” clause; Alarm Agent pattern of past reject spikes linked to leaking valves; no current alarm but reject count rising.)
- Difference vs history: previous events triggered an under‑fill alarm at the moment the reject rate spiked; this occurrence shows a rising reject count without any alarm, indicating the fault is developing but has not yet reached alarm trigger.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: potential quality degradation; if reject rate continues to rise, line may need to stop for seal replacement (estimated downtime ~1 hour). Currently line remains running.
- Safety risk: LOW (no LOTO required yet, no hazardous condition observed).
- Financial impact: incremental loss from rejected bottles; exact cost not quantifiable from provided data.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- MEDIUM – rising reject count exceeds the SOP early‑warning threshold (>1 reject per 100 bottles in an hour) and matches a known pattern that can lead to under‑fill alarms and line stop if not addressed.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action (follow SOP steps exactly):
  Step 1: Safety – Press STOP (normal stop), put on required PPE (safety shoes, cut‑resistant gloves, safety glasses, hearing protection), and apply LOTO as per SAF‑003 before any inspection.
  Step 2: Diagnosis – Read the checkweigher report to identify which valve(s) are under‑filling; inspect those valves for dripping.
  Step 3: Fix – If any valve is dripping, call maintenance to replace the seal kit (WI‑FL101‑001) using the documented seal‑replacement procedure. If no dripping, lock out the machine and clean the nozzle of the under‑filling valve.
  Step 4: Verify – After seal replacement or nozzle cleaning, perform the mandatory first‑bottle check (weigh first 20 bottles; all must be 495‑505 ml). Confirm no under‑fill alarms for at least one hour of production.
  Step 5: Quality – Quarantine any bottles produced since the reject count began to rise; re‑weigh a sample batch and document results in the quality log.

- Root cause fix (permanent solution): Replace worn fill‑valve seals according to the service interval (every 3 months or 1 500 running hours) and ensure fill‑time setting remains at the factory‑specified 3.2 s (do NOT adjust fill time).

- Preventive action: 
  - Add a real‑time reject‑count monitor to alert shift lead when count exceeds 1 % before an alarm triggers. 
  - Enforce the seal‑service interval and record seal‑replacement dates in the maintenance log. 
  - Reinforce SOP training on “do NOT increase fill time” and early‑warning response.

- Who to notify: Shift lead, Maintenance Supervisor, Quality Lead, and Engineering (for schedule review).

12.4 Product Supply Pressure Low
Alarm message: "Product supply pressure low — below 1.3 bar"

Low supply pressure makes bottles underfill.

Causes, most common first:
  1. Supply filter blocked — clean or replace the filter (FLT-PS-10)
  2. Air in the supply line — bleed the air using the bleed valve on the bowl
  3. Supply tank running low — check the tank level with the water
     treatment room

  Step 3 — Bleed air from the supply line.

KNOWLEDGE GRAPH FOR FL-101 — human-reviewed facts, each with its source.

FAULT: Underfill  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 11 and 12.1]
  early warning: If the checkweigher rejects more than 1 bottle in 100 over an hour, tell the shift lead. A rising reject count is often the first sign of worn seals.
  correct response: Press STOP (normal stop, not the emergency stop unless someone is in danger). Dripping valve: call the maintenance technician to replace the seal kit using WI-FL101-001. No dripping: lock out the machine and clean that valve's nozzle. Then check the product supply pressure.
  alarm message: Fill level low — bottles under target volume
  first check: Read the checkweigher report: it shows which valve numbers are underfilling. Look at those valves for dripping.
  causes in order: 1. Worn fill valve seal (the valve drips between fills). 2. Blocked fill nozzle (no dripping). 3. Low product supply pressure (see Product Supply Pressure Low).
  frequency: The most common alarm on FL-101
  alarm trigger: The alarm starts when the checkweigher rejects 3 underfilled bottles in a row
  wrong response: increase the fill time to make up for underfill. It hides worn seals and causes overflow and spillage (NCR-2026-012)
  systemic rule: Three or more underfill alarms in one shift means a systemic fault, usually several worn seals. Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor.
  definition: A bottle with less than 495 ml
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Volume Specification: allowed range: 495 to 505 ml — the checkweigher rejects anything outside this; hourly check: Every hour, take 5 bottles off the line and weigh them by hand; all must be in range; checkweigher test: Before starting, the 490 ml and 510 ml test bottles must be rejected and the 500 ml bottle must pass. If not, do not start: call the quality lead.; target: 500 ml  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.4, 10 and 11]
  SPECIFICATION — Fill Time Setting: rule: The fill time must NOT be changed by operators. Changing it needs written approval from engineering. A longer fill time does not fix underfill: it hides the real cause and makes bottles overflow.; setting: 3.2 seconds, factory set  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 10]
  Possible causes:
    - Worn Fill Valve Seal  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 8.1 and 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Sections 3 and 9, NCR-2026-012 Section 5]
        service interval: Every 3 months or 1,500 running hours, whichever comes first
        check: The checkweigher report shows which valves are underfilling. A valve that drips between fills has a worn seal.
        symptom: The valve drips between fills
        signs of wear: Flattened on one side, small cracks at the edge, hard instead of soft, a groove in the sealing face, discoloured or swollen
        ncr reference: NCR-2026-012: seals on valves 7, 12, 13 and 19 were 900 running hours past the 1,500-hour limit
        many worn: If more than 4 seals are badly worn at the same time, tell the maintenance supervisor: the replacement interval may be too long
        part: SEAL-FV-24
            minimum stock: 10 kits
            description: Fill valve seal kit: main seal and O-ring, one per valve
            location: Filling Line 1 spares cabinet, shelf 2
        fix: Fill Valve Seal Replacement  [source: WI-FL101-001 Sections 2 to 8 and 11]
            lubricant rule: Only food-grade lubricant FGL-1. Any other lubricant contaminates the product.
            when to replace: A valve drips between fills; the checkweigher shows the same valve underfilling again and again; three or more underfill alarms in one shift; or the seal has reached 3 months or 1,500 running hours
            before you start: Check the checkweigher report to see which valves are underfilling, mark them with a green tag, and tell the shift lead how long the line will be stopped
            signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check before normal production restarts. Record the date, valve numbers, seal kits used, condition of the old seals, first-bottle results and your name in the maintenance log.
            steps: 1. Press STOP and lock out the machine (LOTO). 2. Drain the bowl until the product is below the valve level. 3. Remove the valve with the valve key (quarter turn to the left). 4. Remove the old seal and O-ring with the seal pick. 5. Wipe the valve seat clean with a lint-free cloth and check it for scratches. 6. Fit the new seal and O-ring from the SEAL-FV-24 kit with a thin layer of FGL-1 lubricant. 7. Refit the valve (quarter turn to the right until it clicks). 8. Count the tools and parts on the tray, remove the lock and refill the bowl. 9. Sanitation rinse (mandatory). 10. First-bottle check (mandatory).
            reference: WI-FL101-001
            important note: For the first 2 to 3 minutes after a seal change, bottles may be slightly overfilled (up to 510 ml) while the new seals settle. This is EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR — not a fault. Do not change any settings.
            scratched seat: A scratched valve seat must be reported to the maintenance supervisor: a new seal will not seal on a scratched seat
            time: One valve about 15 minutes; a typical job (1 to 4 valves) 30 to 45 minutes
            total downtime: about 1 hour including the rinse and the first-bottle check
            who: Trained maintenance technicians only
            then required: Sanitation Rinse  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 9, FL-101-SOP Sections 4, 9, 12.3 and 17]
                method: Rinse the bowl, valves and nozzles with clean water for 10 minutes. This removes lubricant and particles from the new seals.
                also required: At start-up if the machine has been stopped for more than 4 hours, after glass breakage, and at the end of every shift
                mandatory: true — never skip it after a seal change: the first bottles would carry lubricant into the product
            then required: First-Bottle Check  [source: WI-FL101-001 Step 10 and Section 11]
                method: Run at normal speed and weigh the first 20 bottles. All 20 must be between 495 and 505 ml. If any bottle is outside this range, stop and check the valve again.
                signoff: The shift supervisor signs off the first-bottle check
                mandatory: true — normal production must not restart without it
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003)  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 6.2]
                lock rule: Only the person who fitted a lock may remove it
                required before: Any maintenance, clearing a jam, changing parts, or reaching into the machine
                steps: 1. Switch off power at the main isolator. 2. Lock the isolator with your personal padlock. 3. Tag it with your name and the date. 4. Try to start the machine to prove it cannot run.
        known pattern: Fill Time Trap  [source: NCR-2026-012 Sections 5 and 8]
            chain: Worn seals drip → underfill alarms → fill time raised 3.2 → 3.6 → 3.9 s → most valves overflow → spillage and wet labels → 1,200 bottles rejected, 2 hours 10 minutes downtime
            correct response: Underfill is a seal problem until proven otherwise: check for dripping valves first and replace worn seals (WI-FL101-001). Leave the fill time at the factory setting.
            wrong response: raise the fill time to fix underfill
            description: The operator raises the fill time to make up for underfill caused by worn seals, and most valves then overflow
            lesson from: NCR-2026-012, night shift of 16 January 2026
    - Blocked Fill Nozzle  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
        symptom: The valve underfills but does not drip: debris in the nozzle
        fix: Fill Nozzle Cleaning  [source: FL-101-SOP Section 12.1 Step 4, WI-FL101-001 Section 10]
            method: Lock out the machine and clean the nozzle of the underfilling valve
            then required: LOTO (SAF-003) (details above)
  pattern: Fill Time Trap (details above)
  pattern: Systemic Underfill Indicator  [source: FL-101-SOP Sections 12.1 and 13, NCR-2026-012 Section 8]
      correct response: Stop production, raise a maintenance work order and call the maintenance supervisor
      meaning: Several worn seals: a systemic fault, not bad luck

- DemoBottling‑Shift‑Log‑2026‑09‑01‑Day.csv – prior reject‑count rise pattern
- FL‑101‑Work‑Instruction.txt – seal‑replacement criteria (3 months or 1,500 h)
- Knowledge‑graph entries – fault definition, specifications, cause hierarchy, safety rules (all TIER 1 VERIFIED)

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: early stage of worn fill‑valve seals indicated by a creeping reject count, matching the SOP‑defined early warning that “a rising reject count is often the first sign of worn seals.” (Evidence: SOP, knowledge graph, prior shift logs)
- Difference from historical pattern: previous incidents showed an immediate under‑fill alarm and visible valve dripping; this shift shows only a reject‑count rise with no alarm or observed dripping, indicating the fault is developing earlier than before.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: quality degradation now; if trend continues it will trigger an under‑fill alarm and may require line stop for seal replacement (estimated downtime ~1 hour including LOTO, sanitation rinse, and first‑bottle check).
- Safety risk: LOW (no immediate hazard; standard LOTO and PPE required for any maintenance)
- Financial impact: potential loss from rejected product (reject rate >1 % could cost several thousand dollars per shift) and possible hour of downtime if seals are replaced.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- MEDIUM – rising reject count is a quality warning that can lead to production stop; no safety event or alarm yet, but recurrence risk warrants prompt action.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action:
  Step 1: Safety – Press the normal STOP button, then apply LOTO according to SAF‑003 (switch off main isolator, lock, tag with name/date, verify lockout).
  Step 2: Diagnosis – Read the checkweigher report to identify any valve numbers showing under‑fill rejects.
  Step 3: Inspection – Visually inspect the identified valves:
    - If a valve is dripping between fills, treat it as a worn seal and proceed to seal replacement (see Step 4).
    - If no dripping, lock out the machine (already done) and clean the nozzle of that valve (per SOP Section 12.1).
  Step 4: Fix – For dripping valves, replace the fill‑valve seal kit (SEAL‑FV‑24) following WI‑FL101‑001 steps 1‑10 (LOTO, drain bowl, remove valve, replace seal with food‑grade lubricant FGL‑1, re‑fit valve, remove lock, refill, sanitation rinse, first‑bottle check).
  Step 5: Verify – After any repair or cleaning, run the first‑20‑bottle check; all bottles must be 495–505 ml. Record results and have the shift supervisor sign off.
  Step 6: Quality – Quarantine any bottles produced since the reject count began until the first‑bottle check passes.
- Root cause fix (permanent solution): Replace all worn fill‑valve seals before they exceed 3 months or 1,500 running hours; do not adjust fill time as a workaround.
- Preventive action: Implement a daily reject‑count review; if rejects exceed 1 per 100 bottles in any hour, notify shift lead and schedule seal inspection. Adjust maintenance interval to 2 months or 1,000 h if wear trends accelerate. Record seal‑replacement dates in the maintenance log.
- Who to notify: Shift lead, Maintenance Supervisor, Quality Lead, and Engineering (for interval review).

RISK IF NOT ACTIONED: Continued rejects will trigger an under‑fill alarm, force an unplanned line stop, and increase waste and downtime.

12.4 Product Supply Pressure Low
Alarm message: "Product supply pressure low — below 1.3 bar"

Low supply pressure makes bottles underfill.

Causes, most common first:
  1. Supply filter blocked — clean or replace the filter (FLT-PS-10)
  2. Air in the supply line — bleed the air using the bleed valve on the bowl
  3. Supply tank running low — check the tank level with the water
     treatment room

Immediate action:
  Step 1 — Press STOP.
  Step 2 — Clean the supply filter.
  Step 3 — Bleed air from the supply line.
  Step 4 — Confirm the pressure is back to 1.5 to 2.0 bar.
  Step 5 — Restart, then weigh the first 20 bottles. All must be 495 to 505 ml.
